Building upon Chevalley's seminal constructions of strictly convex, flat tori, we create distinct, strictly convex shapes to demonstrate the spectral discreteness and derive precise lower bounds for the Weyl asymptotics harmonics counts. Our methods can be generalized to analyze subgroups of isometries with non-trivial toric fixed points on these manifolds.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, we investigate a scenario in which the elementary sector comprises a complex scalar field that transforms as a sextet under $U(1)_c$. This setup enables $U(1)_c$ dark force symmetry, allowing us to explore dark matter properties within this framework, guided by experimental constraints. As a result of symmetry breaking, a pseudo-Goldstone boson emerges that can be considered as a dark axion. Our analysis reveals that the dark matter can satisfy all requirements if the hexaton's mass falls within the 10 GeV to 1000 GeV range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed dark axion can account for the entire stellar evolution halos, including the observed lack of an $L_*$ cut in the stellar cores of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, under frequencies $\sim 10^{-9}$ or higher.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to increase walking distances or hide the presence of virtual objects through manipulations in headsets and handheld devices. Nevertheless, manipulating virtual physical entities can also have unintended side effects, such as visible floor distortions, which can decrease users' comfort and walking distances by triggering a heightened state of self-consciousness. Despite our understanding of these manipulations often being effective in holding up user attention, their potential to combine in order to overcome their individual limitations has yet to be fully explored. Unlike past studies, variations in user characteristics or settings can also affect the system's outcome, albeit to a lesser extent. In our investigation, variations of these manipulations and simultaneous presentations of them are being tested to determine their individual and combined effects on users' behavior and increasing their learning and transfer. By utilizing a virtual manipulation of a virtual box that appears to be floating in mid-air using a physical manipulator to oscillate a tether attached to a handheld haptic device, our research indicates that the simple manipulation increases users' interaction time. Furthermore, the most effective strategies were when these manipulations were presented individually, rather than simultaneously, and when they were presented individually, rather than individually.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using the VLT/INTERFEROMETER have revealed the mass distribution of young binary stars. To understand the mass distribution of these systems stellar formation models must be developed. The calculations presented here utilize the smoothed particle hydrodynamics method to simulate the formation of stellar binaries. The formation models take into account various parameters, including the velocity field around colliding supersounds within a rotating, magnetized cloud core. The calculations show that the mass distribution of these systems is influenced by the total mass (M_<0.3M_>) and that the mass distribution of equal-mass binaries decreases as the total mass is reduced. Furthermore, the mass distribution also depends on how rapidly angular momentum is transferred and that the angular momentum transferred in early stages of stellar formation may not always be the initial angular momentum of the cloud core.

This research introduces the \textit{m-arctan Kernel Kernel Fisher Discriminant Independent Component Analysis (m-ar-K-FastICA)} approach for extracting features from datasets with non-Gaussian distributions using arrow function arctangent kernels. It integrates the capabilities of arctangent kernel independent component analysis (ICA), its generalized nonlinear extension, and Fisher Discriminant Analysis to maximize both component independence and class separability. To address data non-stationarity, we modify the existing algorithm by combining the arctangent function with a linear and kernel-based discriminant analysis, thereby combining blind source separation and supervised feature extraction. Furthermore, we develop a reduced computation variant, \textit{(\textit{m}-ar-K-FastICA)} and demonstrate its efficacy through a series of experiments comparing its results to existing methods. Our findings show that this approach outperforms others in terms of classification accuracy, especially for classes with non-Gaussian data.

This paper builds upon existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational complexity. Specifically, choosing non-isomorphic graph identification in Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) and the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus (EPC) yields the same computational bounds. As a direct consequence, since EPC reflects CPT's ability to solve specific decision problems, this link allows us to use EPC as a model-theoretic tool to understand the computational power of algebraic proof systems. Furthermore, this relationship enables a straightforward proof that EPC satisfies a property known as the lemma property, previously established under more complex conditions.

A subring collection in a ring is an extensive set that completely covers the ring when adding together any two elements. The smallest number of subrings needed to cover an ring is called its covering number. In this study, the covering numbers of certain rings, such as integer matrices and p-adic integers, are specifically calculated.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a diverse array of posts that can be categorised into various formats such as text, images, and videos. Given the sheer volume and variety presented, manually verifying the credibility of each piece becomes an almost insurmountable task. To tackle this challenge, we propose an automated method for social fact-checking which hinges on multi-task learning and graph neural networks to bolster the reliability of our predictions. By leveraging multiple objectives during training, our approach effectively aggregates information from distinct domains, thereby enhancing performance across different factors. We validate our solution using the mainstream English databases, yielding substantial improvements.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographic locations is crucial for tracking protests, disasters, breaking news, and more. Unlike static social media data, dynamic data streams require dynamic thresholds for event detection, which can be further complicated by the lack of labeled training data. In this study, an adaptive Bayesian optimization algorithm is proposed to automatically adjust these thresholds on dynamic Twitter streams, using the Twitter API to process 1.5 million tweets per day for a three-month period. The results show that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of F1 score and is able to effectively adapt to different data streams. The source code and data used in the study are available on GitHub.

We introduce a new method to analyze and constrain cosmological parameters, combining the power spectrum and two-point shear convergence correlation function. This technique uses the weighted skew-spectrum, which combines information from the power spectrum and two-point correlation function, with information from the power spectrum at specific, equally spaced w values. This approach maintains information at lower w values, similar to the two-point correlation function, while also incorporating a broader range of information similar to the power spectrum. This method is particularly useful in analyzing mock data from the Euclid and Y3 simulations and has been found to provide comparable or better results than other methods in several configurations and has even better performance when applied to combined datasets of light and dark matter datasets. This technique is particularly useful as a complementary approach to deep learning-based estimation methods due to its transparency.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused significant disruption, including the outbreak of online rumors. To comprehend and control the dissemination of these rumors, we developed a comprehensive framework that bridges online and offline spaces by incorporating real-world road networks and social media's impact on interpersonal communications. Through this approach, we constructed a new model that incorporates interplay among online and offline spaces to map the flow of information and its real-world consequences. To determine the critical nodes driving rumor propagation, we devised a novel index that balances road networks and online social networks' topology, which surpasses existing indices in effectively pinpointing key rumor disseminators. Moreover, we validated our model and conducted numerical experiments based on actual data to evaluate its accuracy and create an innovative strategy for stopping rumor propagation by prioritizing high-index nodes with substantial correct information. Our results demonstrated that this strategy outperforms current approaches in maximizing the coverage of correct information and controlling rumor propagation by a substantial margin.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks, focusing on high bands that carry significant information, illustrated using scenes from urban, rural, and mixed environments. We compare several dimensionality reduction methods, such as PCA, KSVD, ICA, and HCA, focusing on their computational efficiency and effectiveness in real-time applications. To evaluate classification performance, we used popular classifiers including KNN, SVM, and MAXVERB, along with metrics like pixel-wise and node-wise accuracy. We analyzed how compression rates affect classification performance and found that PCA achieves the highest compression with a 0.97% accuracy, while node-wise performance shows slower decline with increased compression. We observed that PCA facilitates real-time classification, whereas other classifiers face latency issues due to their dependence on the entire dataset, making PCA a more suitable method for time-critical applications.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors, but they often suffer from
issues of overfitting and inefficiency, as network size doesn't necessarily correlate
with performance. To address this, researchers introduced the lottery ticket hypothesis,
which suggests that trained networks contain sparse sub-networks of minimal size that
can achieve the optimal fit. To find these sub-networks, we developed an innovative
approach by framing the issue as feature co-training and introducing LTISYNC, which
simultaneously identifies sparse networks and their optimal training parameters through
adapting ISING model techniques. Our method outperforms current approaches, improving
accuracy by 0.5 to 4 percent and achieving more precise sub-network findings in comparison
to prior work.

A novel and precise method, PCS-Proline, has been developed to determine amide proton chemical shift positions in proteins with a spin label attached to a proline residue. This method utilizes the known rigid structure of the connector between amide protons and the spin label to accurately calculate the isotropic magnetic susceptibility tensor. By using high-resolution NMR data, the average susceptibility tensor is determined and then used to predict amide proton chemical shifts for specific residues near the spin label. The predicted shifts agree well with experimental data for various proteins and peptides, including small caicinin, large PCS-Proline protein, and 40-mer peptide. Notably, the agreement between predicted and experimental chemical shifts is within 0.1 ppm, leading to faster structure searches through Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations by directly considering both amide proton and methyl proton chemical shifts during simulations. This technique has significant implications for protein structure determination through NMR.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as crucial in creating robust models for classification tasks. Despite its significance, there has been limited theoretical understanding of how different loss functions influence the learning process in deep neural networks. In this study, we used a Bayesian framework to analyze the theoretical loss landscape of a neural network with quadratic activation and explored the posterior distribution over weights when using two distinct loss functions: cross-entropy and Bayes risk. By applying this approach, we were able to investigate how the loss function influences training in such networks and provide explicit formulas describing the loss landscape. Our findings from theoretical analysis and controlled experiments indicate that the type of loss function used can impact general performance, particularly when optimizing hyperparameters like regularization. The results also highlight the complexity of the loss landscape increases with neural network complexity, rendering the derivation of theoretical landscapes impractical for more complex models.

Describing the highly interconnected states within many-body systems is a significant obstacle in physics. In the realm of interacting fermion systems, quasiparticle behavior dominates, making pairwise correlations the primary focus. By employing the parquet theory, which forms the backbone of modern many-body theory, one can better understand complex system dynamics. Originally, this method involved solving an infinite set of integro-differential equations for bound states, later simplified with the application of specific approximation schemes. However, such approaches often led to spurious results, disregarding key principles. In this study, we utilize the configuration interaction QMC (caDMC) method to directly computationally test pairwise correlation effects within a simplified two-dimensional fermion system, thereby thoroughly evaluating the validity of the modern many-body framework. By comparing multiple correlation metrics, we identify significant discrepancies between parquet components and pinpoint specific terms requiring revision. These findings space correlation effects to a level, four times the energy scale of the system, significantly surpassing conventional many-body theory limits.

Theoretically, we propose that at zero Kelvin, a semimetal can transform into an excitonic insulator through total condensation of electron-hole pairs. This insulator is characterized by a nonzero electron-hole pairing amplitude, unique electron density, uncompensated electron-hole charge density, and nonzero hole density. Furthermore, the Higgs mode of the electron-hole pairing field is identified as a longitudinal oscillation of electron and hole densities. By studying the exciton gas, which could form at high electron-hole doping densities with large interlayer spacing, we find that it can transition into this proposed excitonic insulator state.

In the US, community safety groups use a reporting system to link users to emergency response personnel based on reported incidents. However, a significant problem exists within these services due to limited availability of emergency response personnel, resulting in high reliance on text-based communication which can lead to various issues. To investigate this problem, we created a dataset consisting of real-world reports from community safety programs, and analyzed the decision-making processes of emergency personnel in handling reported incidents through text. Our analysis of community safety program data revealed that text-based communication can be confusing and frustrating for users, and therefore we used an approach to investigate how emotional support provided by dispatchers influences decision-making processes and identified key factors affecting the performance of emergency response personnel.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with magnetically-doped and nonmagnetic-blank flake comparisons, we conducted magnetization-dependent $\mu$SR studies. By examining two samples of different thickness, we found a substantial, vortex-like field dependence that significantly influences the muon spin depolarization, leading to two distinct transition temperatures in the spin depolarization profile. Notably, this influence of vortex-like fields is found in both samples, its effects however diminish as the sample thickness decreases. By investigating the spatial distribution of magnetic fields using muon stopping depths, we determined that vortices originate from the sample surface area, displaying no indications of internal magnetic bias within the magnetically-doped samples. Furthermore, through detailed analysis of how the muon stopping depth distribution changes with depth, we were able to estimate the in-plane vortex flux per unit area and infer the superconducting critical current density in the top surface of both samples. By comparing the critical current densities, we found that current carried by superconducting order in the top surface is enhanced by magnetic doping. By contrasting this with transport measurements, we found that magnetic doping does not suppress the transition temperature in the bulk of the sample. By comparing with theoretical calculations, we found that this transition temperature is consistent with that predicted by mean-field theory in case the magnetic impurities introduce pair-breaking via Ising-type spin-anisotropy and that the transition temperature in the bulk

Label-efficient active learning techniques select critical unlabeled samples to reduce annotation costs. Traditional methods focus on two key approaches: choosing representative or challenging examples. However, there has been a lack of structured analysis on the representative labeling strategy. This study addresses this gap by systematically examining the representative labeling technique, defining its core principles and proposing initial unifiers under these principles. An in-depth comparison of representative and uncertainty-based sampling strategies reveals that the latter is excludable in favor of the former. Not only does this study introduce specific types of sample adaptivity and redundancy elimination unified strategies, but it also critically evaluates the effectiveness of current unified and representative sampling methods. Consequently, the study offers valuable insights and recommendations for future research in active learning to improve model training performance.

To study how music has evolved over time, we need a numerical indicator of musical characteristics that can track secular changes within large music collections. By employing a novel metric named "loudness complexity," which evaluates how dynamic elements like drums and vocals affect the overall intensity of a song, we've investigated their progression across more than one million songs spanning six decades. We discovered that the average intensity of songs has significantly increased since the 1960s, with each decade bringing an 11% rise, leading to approximately an 80% increase since then. Surprisingly, this increase in intensity is consistent across all genres, although various factors contribute to the observed trends.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves continuous-time arrangements of random blocks or 'clusters'. In these processes, there is a non-zero probability that an individual unit within a block will switch to another, previously formed, block, based upon the same criteria as the initial selection process. The probability of switching a number to an existing block is directly related to the block's size and is represented by a continuous, non-decreasing function applied to the block's size. This is in contrast to traditional stochastic partition processes, where the probability of switching occurs according to a predetermined rule. When considering two specific types of processes - one based on 'sticky' random walks and the other on 'rank-dependent' processes, notable relationships can be established, notably between the expected block sizes across varying parameters. These processes encompass well-known concepts such as coalescing random walks, 'Chinese restaurant processes', and 'bursts', upon reaching maturity. The research delves into establishing correspondence between certain properties of these processes through a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. The findings reveal the existence of a uniform convergence phenomenon in the distribution of block sizes as the population size increases to infinity, thereby unifying two distinct families of models under a singular framework and enabling examination of the asymptotic behavior in a more targeted manner. The paper's primary objective lies in investigating the statistical distribution of block sizes as the population size approaches infinity. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data simulation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method to be comparable to individual feedback provided to offline policy reward models, using the same total human labeling effort.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that any such configurations can be used to construct a steady state ideal magnetic plasma in the presence a constant external magnetic field. Notably, the electric current density associated with these configurations exhibits a distribution concentrated in point singularities and directed curves.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, applying Bayes' Theorem to treat TTYL as a treatment and Age as a confounder, resulting in an expression for TTYL's population treatment effect that relies on individual treatment propensity. Estimators derived from this equation, such as AIPW and nAIPW, exhibit key properties like consistency and double robustness, making them suitable for simulation-based inference. However, given the finite sample size, simulating the ATE in two steps often introduces significant bias. An alternative approach that minimizes this bias involves an alternative estimator, "STYBI," which can be theoretically and empirically justified as a direct estimator of the ATTE. In contrast to AIPW and nAIPW, STYBI exhibits reduced bias and reduced variance in simulations, although it does not possess consistency or double robustness properties.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in b-hadron decays, which is suspected to be a sign of beyond-Standard Model new physics. To better understand the underlying mechanism responsible for these violations, which new physics could be affecting not only $b$-decays but also $\tau$ decays, a new study is set to explore the difference in time between preferred decays of charged $\tau$ particles. Two particular decay modes of $\tau$ will be in focus: $\tau \to 3l$ (with $l$ being either $e$ or $m$) and $\tau \to \nu \gamma$. To determine whether these differences can be a sign of new physics, which could be helping to connect the dots between $b$-decay anomalies and upcoming data from Belle II, a theoretical framework is developed using both vector and scalar types of new physics. While the choice of interaction within this framework is flexible and not strictly determined, which influences the difference in time between preferred decays but not ratios of hadronic decay widths in $b$-decay, the differences in these two types of interactions can provide a more comprehensive picture when considered together.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, which are crucial to atmospheric circulation. The laboratory model enables researchers to control these factors in a consistent manner to better understand the general circulation characteristics of the atmosphere. In order to measure variability in general circulation patterns, we applied novel signal processing and machine learning approaches to annulus setup signal data, ensuring minimal data preprocessing is required. The analysis reveals that a combined technique of empirical mode decomposition and Fisher projection outperforms both principal component analysis and convolutional autoencoders with little data tuning, requiring only a sample size of 200 for 95% accuracy in general variability recognition. The effectiveness of this method is validated by its ability to generalize well on a large test dataset consisting of nearly 2000 examples, achieving approximately 97% classification accuracy in laboratory settings.

In a study, we investigate the limitation of parametric threshold models for identifying tail risks. To solve this issue, we apply a threshold-invariant extreme value model, also known as the shape and scale model. Using H\u{a}rdle and Linton's separation approach, we handle large datasets and provide a likelihood-free estimation method with reduced computational complexity. Our results show that this model outperforms the Generalized Pareto Function approach in terms of risk assessment accuracy, even with large-scale data.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we establish a theoretical framework that can recover near-optimal policies even when an adversary has modified a fraction $\delta$ of the data tuples. By developing a robust value estimation method, each policy we propose guarantees a level of performance that is only marginally less than the best possible one, with the margin dependent on $\delta$ and the policy's action entropy. Using this framework, we can recover nearly-optimal policies in a modified version of the robust MDP problem, and further explore its application to a variant involving entropy regularization.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

We're seeing an increased presence of artificial molecular motors that operate via
stimulation by electric currents over a wide range of powers, offering unique
capabilities at the molecular level. Despite extensive research on their designs, the
specific impact of different types of electric fields on these devices remains unclear,
mainly due to the difficulty in measuring them experimentally. To address this, we've
applied advanced simulation techniques to examine the workings of artificial motors,
specifically those based on the research of Delgado and co-workers, previously discussed in their 2019 publication.

Building on a 2013 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite field $\mathbb{F}$, denoted as $V = \mathbb{F}^n$, and a function $f$ that maps elements of $V$ to $\mathbb{F}$. Through point-wise multiplication of functions $g, h: V \rightarrow \mathbb{F}$, their convolution, denoted as $g \star_h f$, is a function that takes an element $u \in (\mathbb{F}^n)^2$ and returns the sum of the products $f(u_i x_i)h(x)$, where $u_i$ are the entries of $u$. A brute-force approach allows us to compute all values of the convolution $f \star g$ in $| \mathbb{F} |^{4n}$ time. In this study, we focus on the input size $n$ and field $\mathbb{F} = \{0, 1\}$, where we design an algorithm with time $2^{O(n)}$ for computing a single value of the convolution. In our approach, we reduce the problem to instance translation of Toffoli gates, where we show that translating $k$ gates can be done in time $2^{O(k)}$, thus establishing a computational bound of computing the convolution in time $n^{O

For several decades, the L dwarf candidate GJ 229B has been studied, but 
retrospective analysis of observational data from 1995 reveals our initial 
spectrum observations were incomplete and misleading for the system. We 
performed a comprehensive re-examination of all available spectral data from 
ultraviolet to mid-infrared ranges to accurately retrieve the physical 
properties of GJ 229B. Our approach involved using multiple models updated to 
reflect the latest in exoplanete science to determine how different 
wavelengths contribute to understanding GJ 229B. Our results indicate GJ 229B 
has a mass of 29-65 times the mass of Jupiter, an initial estimate that 
resolves the long-standing mass discrepancy, and we find GJ 229B has an 
effective temperature of 650-750K, which confirms the cool atmosphere of 
GJ 229B is dominated by water vapor and alkaline earth metals. Our 
characterization of GJ 229B using a broad spectral range demonstrates 
completeness of brown dwarf spectral analysis and emphasizes the need for 
broadband or broad spectral range analysis in exoplanete and brown dwarf 
science.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we employed the systematic approach using 4D flow equations. The type of state we're searching for might be represented by the interaction between a nucleon and antinucleon, specifically $N\bar{N}$. However, the results from the $\bar{p}p$ system at centre-of-mass energies up to 2 GeV reveal no evidence of a resonance corresponding to this state. Additionally, we looked for the $0^{--}$ state in the interaction involving a nucleon and a lambda particle, $N\Lambda$, but a detailed analysis of these centre-of-mass energies up to 2.5 GeV also fails to confirm its presence.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}\bar{c}u$ decays. The primary methods to achieve this goal involve analyzing the decay $\bar{B}^0_{d}\to K^{+}\mu^{-}\bar{\nu}_{\mu}$ and $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ and examining the correlations of final-state particles within muon-producing $\bar{B}^0_{d}\to K^{-}\mu^{+}\bar{\nu}_{\mu}$ and $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decays. The research also explores the dependence of these correlations on the pseudoscalar and vector mode $\bar{B}^0\to h\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ ($h=P$ or $K^{*0}$) transitions on the muon's pseudoscalar decay parameter $\phi_{s}$. Airborne transmission risk assessment requires a detailed understanding of how virus-laden aerosols move within confined environments. This is influenced by building design, interior layout, and the movement of people within that layout. Building on previous research into particle diffusion, our work develops an expanded approach that takes into account the impact of occupant movements and how they correlate with instantaneous particle distribution. This new method allows for a more nuanced modeling of infectious aerosols, supplementing existing research that typically focuses on infectious particles themselves.

This study has examined $\beta$-decay related characteristics between specific isotopes of Ni, Pd, and Ru within the $0^-$ to $2^+$ energy range using shell-model based calculations. By comparing theoretical and experimental $\beta$-decay properties, this work also investigated the $\beta$-decay of a recently created, highly $\beta$-unstable isotope of Ni.

Double-sided auctions are widely used in financial markets for executing multiple quantities of trade. Recent research offers methods for conducting double-sided auctions with multiple quantity trade, but these methods have been limited to markets for transferable goods, making them inapplicable to transferable digital assets like tokens. Our study aims to adapt and extend these methods to accommodate non-transferable transactions, making them suitable for use in liquidity-providing mechanisms like blockchain-based order books. We evaluate the proposed method's efficacy in achieving optimal price and ensuring market clearability through extensive numerical experiments. Moreover, we develop an algorithm using side-by-side matching that ensures clear pricing of the order book in a computationally efficient manner.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we were able to estimate their decay times. Our research further included an analysis of the $F$-wave charmed mesons, which provided a basis for comparing the decay times of various mesons within the same category. The outcomes of our research are discussed and presented.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic setting. Following this, a periodic investigation is examined, and the nonexpansive lines within this context are characterized. In addition, a periodic theorem related to the kernel's nonexpansiveness is shown to be equivalent to a particular problem in additive combinatorics, which involves Michalka's equation. Finally, the authors establish results that allow for a understanding of the lines that meet the criteria of Szalka's theorem.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity. The dynamic mode decomposition technique, designed to identify linear autonomous systems from observational data, has proven ineffective in addressing these nonlinear systems. However, a new approach proposes using spectral methods to analyze the dynamic modes of nonlinear systems, interpreting dynamic modes as dominant nonlinear resonance phenomena. By applying the technique to model examples, including the Lorenz-96 system, a successful implementation is demonstrated, and theoretical and practical considerations are analyzed.

The timeless appeal of chess lies in its blend of timelessness and evolution,
particularly in the realm of chess openings. Although an immutable game, the way
chess is played has changed significantly over the past two centuries, a change
driven largely by the growing popularity of chess among casual players and the
increased accessibility of opening databases. While experts can offer invaluable
advice through coaching, they are limited by their individual knowledge and the
time-consuming process of staying updated. A new tool has been developed using
machine learning algorithms to create an interactive network of chess openings,
powered by historical game data. The network allows users to explore common
strategies associated with different openings and the trends within them, which
can help players of all skill levels to stay informed about evolving opening
parties and uncover less explored but potentially advantageous alternatives.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

This research focuses on nonlocal constants of motion in systems that lose energy and momentum, applying this framework to mechanics. We derive specific forms of these constants for systems described by second-order differential equations and explore their implications on solution existence and behavior. We also develop new estimates that can help analyze the long-term behavior of orbits in these systems. The study includes examples of applying this framework to three well-known models: the Fokker-Planck equation, a damped oscillators model, and a string dynamics model with nonlocal damping.

Developing free 3D models is extremely time-consuming, making it a daunting task for the general public. To simplify this process, technology like NeRF has made it possible to create scenes from a few photographs, thus reducing the 3D modeling barrier. Nonetheless, producing NeRF still requires some technical expertise and a considerable amount of data collection. In our paper, we introduce an innovative method called air-doodling to collect 3D models by sketching them out in a virtual reality setting, thus making the process more user-friendly. By employing implicit neural representations, our approach lets consumers draw NeRFs implicitly within 3D spaces, essentially making one sketch represent multiple shapes. To enable this concept, we have developed a simple and intuitive VR interface that enables consumers to sketch out neural representations using the handheld controllers and paint them on demand, ultimately represent multiple neural patterns within a single neural space. By utilizing our technique, consumers can produce a vast array of time-efficient, easy-to-use 3D models by simply drawing a宁宁 in 3D space, thus circumventing any need for prior technical knowledge.

KC Systems Inc. is constructing the first direct-drive exoplanet loitering space vehicle using NASA's Breakthrough Starshot technology, to optimize the search for life-like biosignatures in stellar habitable zones. The planet around the star HD 8544, which features a potentially habitable climate, is ideal for this type of search, but requires precise orbital navigation to access its habitable zone. This project is in the early stages of designing a loitering space vehicle to study eccentric orbit dynamics, particularly the prolonged presence at aphelion, where most of the time is spent. These vehicles would gather data on insolation, tidal forces, and radiation to identify safe and stable orbits for extended missions. Due to insolation variations in highly eccentric orbits, significant temperatures are experienced at perihelion, while low temperatures are recorded at aphelion. Due to insensitivity to small amounts of energy, the presence of thermal radiation from low temperatures is more pronounced in the far infrared spectrum. This thermal radiation, though weak, can be detected by advanced telescopes, aiding in the analysis of eccentric orbit stability and the long-term mission of star vehicle observation.

In this study, we are examining a scenario of self-similar gravitational collapse within a perfect fluid. The state of the fluid is governed by a perfect gas equation that accounts for non-zero temperature and variable specific heat capacity. The hydrodynamic equations describing this scenario form a system of nonlinear, coupled partial differential equations, and our analysis focuses on determining which states allow the equations to be consistent with the self-similar collapse profile. The state of the fluid can be characterized by the adiabatic index and a dimensionless parameter related to the equation of state, and our study identifies the regions in this parameter space that result in the hyperbolic type of the hydrodynamic equations, facilitating a method of solution through Riemann invariants. The relationship between the two invariants and the self-similar collapse profile is then explored through the derivation of a system of nonlinear, coupled ordinary differential equations, which can be solved numerically to determine which invariants lead to the consistent gravitational collapse behavior we are interested in. The study reveals that the fluid must be in a thermally collapsing state with stable equilibrium as it moves towards higher density for the equations to be consistent with the self-similar collapse profile.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the extremality bound, the effective stress tensor must satisfy specific energy conditions. We have applied this method to study higher derivative corrections to black holes in known effective actions resulting from string theory and supergravity. Finally, we have verified that linear scalar perturbations on a Kerr black hole obey the weak energy condition.

In reinforcement learning, goal-directed motor learning is accomplished through a two-step process: predicting the value of states under different actions through a neural model, and utilizing policy models that calculate first-order gradients for state updates. Since environmental models are typically inaccurate and their errors are correlated over time, a theory of prediction error decomposition is required to understand how the brain uses these errors effectively. By applying a novel neural decoding method to monitor activity in macaque prefrontal cortex during tasks where error signals were manipulated to mimic real-world conditions, it was discovered that end-effect drives are derived from the total error in action-value predictions, consistent with optimal learning predictions and a rational learning framework.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as an adaptation of the Benincasa model to the context of generalised Poincaré groups.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visual goals in an environment. Existing methods often focus on exploring the global map, but ignore the importance of the local environment, which is also crucial for navigation. Furthermore, they have limited capabilities in adapting to the changing environment. We introduce MemoNav, a novel system that incorporates short-term and long-term memories to manage both local and global environments. We use short-term memory, implemented as circular buffers, to record immediate movement data, while long-term memory, a combination of semantic and radiometric maps, is updated with new information. We employ a semantic module to create a semantic map, updating it with the short-term memory, and a radiometric module, using it to generate a radiometric map. We test MemoNav on multiple datasets, including indoor UCSD and outdoor CLUTRR and St. Andrew's, where we find it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, while also enabling transfer of learning between datasets.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells like femto, pico, and micro cells. However, this initial deployment was constrained by limited licensed spectrum and excessive management overhead, prompting more innovative approaches such as dynamic spectrum access, backharing, and network coordination. Upcoming 5G networks will leverage a more sophisticated nano cell architecture, utilizing intelligent, autonomous technologies to support critical areas such as enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-low latency communications, and high-security mobile networking. The integration of AI/ML and advanced processing frameworks in the 5G era will lead to the development of more efficient and capable systems to meet these requirements.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately demonstrating that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Our work also bridges the concept of Lie symmetry with information capacity, yielding a novel interpretation of symmetry's role in these systems.

Understanding the structural composition of the Hoyle state, a highly excited state of the $^{8}$He nucleus, is crucial in understanding the alpha-cluster nature of nuclei. Since 1985, the nucleus has been studied, but its exact alpha-cluster structure, especially its direct decay into two alpha particles, has not been clearly defined. With recent advancements in the precision of the decay ratio by 2022, new theoretical analysis has been conducted using significant alpha-cluster nuclear models to determine the cluster structure of the Hoyle state. These theories include the Resonating Group Method with 2-particle and 3-body forces, and the Unified Micro-Macro Model, which together suggest that the Hoyle state may not be composed of distinct, weakly-interacting alpha clusters as previously thought, but rather of strongly interacting clusters. This evidence, combined with experimental findings, indicates that the Hoyle state is more accurately described as a cluster of three alpha particles.

In the introduction of this letter, the existing understanding of dynamic crack propagation in 2D brittle materials is reviewed, with a specific focus on the implications of linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) at high-speed crack movement. To illustrate the implications of this focus, two fundamental topics are explored: the instability of cracks during propagation and the application of non-conservative force loading. Consequently, the main conclusions from this review are summarized to highlight the significance of these findings.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels that have memory, utilizing the concept of feedback capacity. The feedback capacity is defined as the highest achievable rate of communication through these channels with the use of feedback in a coding scheme. The relationship between the various lower bounds on feedback capacity and their corresponding upper bounds (including Blum-Kumar's and Cuff's bounds) is examined. The areas of exploration left open by this comparison are identified. The analysis shows that while the two versions of Blum-Kumar's bound yield equivalent outcomes, the gap between Blum-Kumar's and Cuff's upper bounds increases with the size of the alphabet. The article offers a more straightforward method for establishing the monotonicity of the Blum-Kumar bound in relation to the alphabet size.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we investigate the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in two-dimensional attractive Hubbard models with spin and d-wave symmetries, finding that this combination is conducive to the emergence of non-trivial topological spin-orbit coupling and d-wave superconductivity. We further demonstrate that quantum critical phenomena can be induced by adjusting the Zeeman field, leading to competing phase transitions between s-wave and d-wave superconductivity, quantum disorder, and ferromagnetism. The co-existence of non-trivial topology and unconventional superconductivity is found to be resistant to thermal fluctuations.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to understand their structure and content and relate them to natural language. To achieve this, we suggest an approach for assessing knowledge regarding table data and its context in two steps: (1) identifying the source of the information as either a given premise or external knowledge, and (2) verifying the validity of the claim. To support this, we have established a new dataset called TableAuth, consisting of two parts: (1) identifying the source of information as either a given premise or external knowledge, and (2) verifying the validity of the claim. To check the validity of the claim, we have introduced an approach based on the concept of relevance, allowing us to assess whether a claim is relevant to a given table and verify its accuracy based on the information presented in the table. To assist models in making more accurate judgments about verification accuracy, we have introduced a concept of relevance scoring, enabling accurate verification even when a claim is based on external knowledge not contained within the table, which in turn helps improve overall accuracy rates.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this can be called a resolving set, with the smallest such sub-set giving us the metric dimension of the graph. We explore this concept by focusing on a specific subset of vertices, focusing on those with a specific 'order' or distance measure less than or equal to k in the graph, denoted as B_k(G), and examining when this subset can fully identify the whole graph effectively.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing groundwater flow for a recent study in remote areas. Initially, I examined the fundamental conservation laws, specifically mass and energy, to establish a baseline understanding of the problem. I focused on the behavior of these laws over extended time frames and large spatial scales, as relevant to our case. I also considered energy only in its thermal state, ignoring that of mechanical movement. Subsequently, I explored a more detailed examination of the ground's response to stress, which can be relevant to a more precise understanding of the groundwater system. Ultimately, these equations need to be simplified to reach a level of understanding that is both practical and intuitive for our study.

This work presents a detailed examination of the oxidation process of gas-phase pollutants using ozone and ultraviolet (UV) radiation through a mathematical modeling framework. A non-dimensional model describing this interaction between UV and ozone is established, along with a mathematical analysis that ensures the model's solutions are unique and maintain positivity. A numerical solution method is proposed and demonstrated through two distinct scenarios: one involving perfect UV radiation reflection and another without reflection. This demonstration utilizes a real-life case of toluene oxidation in a gas-phase. Furthermore, the study explores the effect of various dimensionless parameters on the model's behavior in these examples.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Nocturne addresses this challenge by being a high-performance, open-source simulator that accurately models analog neural networks and mixed-signal analog-to-digital converters, enabling detailed system-level evaluations of neural and mixed-signal systems. By leveraging multi-core capabilities, Nocturne can run on various computing platforms, allowing for extensive simulations of large neural systems and complete neuromorphic designs, including applications on FPGAs and ASICs.

Decision trees are widely regarded for their ability to provide clear predictive models with easily interpretable structure, yet their standard forms assume certainty in training data, which is often not the case in reality.  Taking into account the presence of uncertain data, we introduce a variation of decision trees known as Indecision Trees, also KNN-CAT Decisions Trees, that can effectively incorporate uncertain training examples.  By doing so, these Decisions Trees can capture the uncertain nature of data and present a more comprehensive representation through the use of an Indecision probability distribution.  Experimental results demonstrate that this innovative approach outperforms traditional Decision Trees when working with data containing uncertain entries and also surpasses some state-of-the-art methods designed to handle uncertain data.

The DTW distance, a widely used measure for time series similarity, has a computationally intensive nature, posing challenges for its application in large datasets and real-time scenarios. To mitigate this issue, a proposed algorithm called EAPrunedDTW combines DTW with a topological data analysis approach to reduce its search space efficiently. By limiting the considered time points between DTW's start and end endpoints, this approach significantly reduces computation time, while still yielding comparable results to standard DTW. Furthermore, the efficacy of EAPrunedDTW in semi-supervised time series classification was evaluated through experiments on multiple datasets, revealing substantial reductions in computation time without compromising classification accuracy. Additionally, a preliminary analysis of DTW's start and end points, utilizing topological properties, showed promising outcomes in accurately predicting target points, potentially further optimizing performance.

Effective testing education can be challenging due to students' common misconceptions. Current teaching tools often fall short as they only present concepts without addressing underlying student difficulties, while available solutions typically lack empirical validation. To bridge this gap, a teaching platform is proposed, utilizing inquiry-based learning to help undergraduate comprehension of testing concepts through interactive learning activities. By analyzing student learning patterns, the system offers a data-driven teaching approach. Experiments using real student data confirm the effectiveness of this approach and the ability to predict student difficulty in testing education. Furthermore, the proposed system represents a novel approach to testing education, with associated datasets and evaluation methods contributing to the field of data-driven testing education.

In domains requiring reliable and transparent machine learning, explainable AI is increasingly utilized to enhance model trustworthiness, pinpoint flaws in predictive patterns, and improve overall decision-making processes. However, the exceptionally high standards for these domains make achieving genuine explanations a significant challenge. Given the lack of clear definitions for explanations in these contexts, we argue that approximate explanations can be more practical and sufficient, if they align with domain-specific constraints (CAPs). Consequently, we introduce a methodology for deriving CAPs from domain experts and utilising them as a filter for selecting the most feasible explanations from a vast array of possible alternatives. This methodology is currently being tested in three distinct domains – public transport demand forecasting, computational pathology, and energy system state estimation – where we are developing and evaluating various explanation methods based on domain-specific requirements.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it.

Dark matter particle research has been conducted using a dataset of Z boson decays into protons or neutrons and a missing momentum entity from a 13 TeV proton-proton collision at the Large Hadronic Collider. Nielsen-Erik Skryberg's standard model interpretation involves analyzing 35.9 fb^-1 of collected data in a 13 TeV proton-proton collision experiment. With a high-confidence level of 95%, the experiment's findings are analyzed using the exclusion method to determine the limits of the dark matter particle interaction cross-section as function of the particle's mass. A Nielsen-Erik-based analysis shows the cross-section limit follows a specific pattern based on the particle's mass within a predetermined range.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, a property that is studied here to determine which spaces possess it. The space βX minus X must be discrete for a space X to have CSHP. The space βX minus X must be discrete for a space X to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be finite for a space to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be finite for a space to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be countably infinite for a space to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be countably infinite for a house to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be countably infinite for a garden to have CSHP. The space of all continuous maps from a space to a discrete space must be countably infinite for a library to have CSHP.
