We introduce HandTrack, an advanced hand joint tracking system specifically designed for ECG data annotation. To address the challenges of deformable hand movements, occlusions, and low resolution in Inverse Kinematics (IK) methods, our innovation involves introducing a canonicalization step. This step transforms the hand pose into a canonical, easy-to-track configuration. To automate hand detection and tracking in raw time series data, we develop a novel hand pose representation model named HandRPE, which functions similarly to Recurrent Pyramid Networks, incorporating a novel influence matrix to combine hand joint activities. We enhance its effectiveness by applying an attention mechanism to filter out irrelevant information. We train our system using labeled Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) data, with results from experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrating the capability of HandRPE to select significant information and accurately track canonical hand pose. With seamless integration with IK modules, the HandTrack system offers a highly accurate and seamless approach to automated hand pose annotation, as verified by validation using gold standard data.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on a single image of a scene, captured without the presence of any additional markers (such as a checkerboard or spherical markers). In contrast to existing markerless approaches, our system's reliability is not compromised by potential biases from object shapes like a person's head or eyes. Instead, we rely solely on the virtual end-effector pose, inferred from eye corners, to accomplish the task. Furthermore, our system's robustness is enhanced by incorporating a global optimisation process, leading to significantly improved results. In practice, our system's calibration can be achieved as quickly as one frame rate, making it extrinsically calibrate the camera in just one second. The significant benefits of this approach in enhancing robustness, simplifying the process, and reducing its setup are substantial, while also requiring minimal equipment - the required setup is equipment-free - nothing more than the user's face.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted using an enhanced framework. In this framework, the interactions of dark matter particles within a star's density are modeled through the scattering of particle pairs, rather than the dark matter particles' direct decay. Ultimately, the star's neutrino production rate will be determined by solving the equations of dark matter particle conservation within a neutron star. These calculations will include the roles of various neutrino channels and the production of bound dark matter states.

The ongoing UCL HiZICS project has made progress in establishing a calibration framework for the cosmological shear estimation code (ctcosmobis), particularly in addressing the UCLASS cosmological simulation. Analytical relationships between the shear estimation bias and the mass map's PSF are derived, enabling the prediction of shear bias from ctcosmobis based on the underlying power spectrum. By comparing this forecast to the results of hi-z fis, a tool for removing shear bias in cosmological shears, we are able to mitigate the bias at a high level of accuracy (less than 0.1%). Furthermore, the removal process also addresses a residual bias that arises due to the rounding of shears in hi-z fis itself. Analysis of hi-z fis's multiplicative shear removal algorithm identifies an unmitigated bias of approximately -50 microarcseconds that is present in the output shears. By combining the insights of ctcosmobis and hi-z fis, we are better positioned to identify the optimal combination of tools to accurately correct shear bias in cosmological shears. With the UCLASS project nearing completion, our findings will provide the foundation for determining the validity of the negative cosmological shear used in BaMIA's code, as well as the accuracy with which it can be calibrated.

A notable consequence of a finding made by V. Berg and S. V. Kozlov in 2019 reveals that, under certain ergodic transformations, specific sets related to irrational rotations exhibit varying degrees of distribution. Notably, in the context of translations on the unit interval, exhibiting such distribution necessitates the presence of a set with non-zero measure, according to V. Berg et al. in all subsequent instances. Our research disproves this universal rule by discovering a dynamically invariant set, whose measure unequivocally amounts to zero, that does exhibit the required degree of distribution.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its zero field magnetic anisotropy of D=0 and specific properties, we were able to accurately determine its BKT field strength (H_BKT=7.8 T) for the first time. Consequently, we were able to refine our two-dimensional cross-field susceptibility plot analysis and thus obtain a more precise estimate of the BKT field (H_BKT'~7.5 T). Notably, we were able to verify that the observed BKT field closely matches the theoretically predicted value of 7.6 T based on the exchange interaction parameters of the material.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum's hierarchy problem. The model's dark matter composition arises from a combination of neutrinos and QCD axions, with the latter being generated through two main pathways: the inflaton decaying into axions and a transfer of an asymmetry from the inflaton to the QCD axion field. The inclusion of radiative axion mass generation also offers an alternative explanation for why their mass is so small. The model can be further enhanced to incorporate on-shell dark matter by adding either a scalar or pseudoscalar portal to dark matter.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for simulating a specific magic state, ultimately revealing that the related existing upper bound grows at a rate of O(m^(1/3) log m), where m represents the number of magic states, surpassing prior knowledge. This discovery enables the expansion of the classically simulable region of circuits with these states. In addition, the research introduces an extension of the shadow tomography method that facilitates the simultaneous estimation of a large number of multi-copy magic states with minimal required measurements.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to examine the evolution of different cosmological phases.
Using the $\rho_{Q}$ based on a reduced phase, we've analyzed critical values of the 
Tsallis parameter $h$ ($0.27 \leq h \leq 1.12$ at $z = 0$) as a boundary for real universe description.
We've investigated the cosmological phase evolution by analyzing key equations of state parameters, 
including whether they describe an interacting or non-interacting universe, and discussed potential effects on cosmic acceleration's future trend.

Between January 2003 and December 2022, the LAMOST survey captured a comprehensive collection of 15,551 low-resolution spectra within the declination range of $-35\degree < \mathrm{Dec} < -30\degree$. This extensive dataset covers a vast area of $22\mathrm{SR}$ and encompasses the diverse Galactic structures of the inner bulge, the disk, and the outer regions. This paper presents the acquisition process and quality assessment of these spectra. Out of the total collection, $86\%$ of the spectra have a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, providing reliable stellar parameter information, spectral classification, and metal abundance data for individual stars or spectroscopic binary systems. Following a rigorous data analysis to eliminate defective spectra, the dataset was refined to 11,681 spectra with high signal-to-noise ratios. These were systematically organized into distinct populations based on their apparent magnitudes and color indices, facilitating further astronomical research on specific stellar populations within these distinct regions.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in embedded systems, SRAM-based TRNGs present an attractive option. Yet, existing TRNGs using SRAM predominantly rely on SRAM's inherent defects, which although convenient can be absent in flawless chips or easily manipulated. In this exploratory study, the potential of SRAM's inherent variations is investigated. Through this analysis, the feasibility of leveraging the variations in SRAM bank select circuitry as an entropy source is shown. In our evaluation, a prototype based on a commercial SRAM and incorporating a linear feedback shift register, as well as a cryptographic hash function, is presented and its output quality is assessed. The results of this evaluation indicate that the variation source based on SRAM bank select circuitry achieves excellent post-processing results, using only 10^4 bytes of output, passing a broad spectrum of statistical quality assessments within 2 seconds.

A pioneering electronic device with the capability to store information was first discovered accidentally. Since then, the underlying mechanisms have been the subject of intense research for over two decades due to the vast possibilities they present. However, the scientific community is still left with numerous unanswered questions about the formation of conductive filaments and the effects of various materials on the process. To address these knowledge gaps, a vast number of experiments are needed to systematically explore the behavior of different molecular assemblies, which is extremely time-consuming and complex due to the effects of many variables on the data collected. Although the conductive filaments are believed to form through electrochemical migration, no materialistic migration has been observed to occur at such small scales. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop novel approaches that not only accelerate the formation of filaments but also enable their efficient erasure, ultimately enabling extremely high-density memory with the combined benefits of volatility and high retention, while also making it possible to store vast amounts of analog data. Traditionally, the creation of filaments is achieved by applying voltage to a material to trigger the migration of ions or neutral species. In this research, the authors present a vast array of molecular assemblies to facilitate resistive switching through purely charge-free mechanisms. The study utilized three distinct materials - one that conducts charge neutrally and two based on polymeric materials that utilize charge-free entanglement and threading - to demonstrate their effects on resistive switching. The resulting devices are minuscule, with sizes smaller than

Using loop-tree duality, we derive a fully explicit formula for the one-loop scattering amplitude in an eikonal approximation from arbitrary irreducible skeleton graphs. One-loop dual tree contributions are defined by pairs of loop cuts yielding tree-level structures, whose numbers match those in equivalent Feynman integral representations. Given that any loop cut separates loops into distinct sets, we formulate a general rule to assign a ordering that expresses amplitude contributions in terms of these cuts, showing that they often correspond to propagator symmetry properties. Furthermore, in theories with Lorentz violation such as ETL, we demonstrate that spurious terms arising in amplitude expressions can be eliminated through the application of LTD to counterterms, while we observe that these spurious terms can be removed in Feynman integral representations via differences that annihilate the amplitude.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable outcomes regarding resolvent expressions and asymptotic behavior of eigenfunctions.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. Through systematic investigation, our findings demonstrate that $q$-deformation's impact is primarily one of magnification, amplifying both optomechanical instability and optically induced transparency transitions. The parameter $q$'s variation has the ability to modify the critical points of optically induced transparency, leading to changes in its transition order from second to fourth order. Additionally, our $q$-deformation framework yields results consistent with standard nonlinear optics when $q$ approaches unity, providing a reliable model for studying this phenomenon.

In a previous study, I developed a model where two rotating rigid rotors interacted through a specific type of coupling. This model, now simplified, allows us to analyze systems composed of two interacting classical bodies represented by the Two-Rotors Model. These, classically, consist of bodies capable of rotating around any axis. Through an exploration, I've identified specific states, known as scissors states, which can be achieved in a specific way. It has also been demonstrated, within a specific framework, how these states can be detected and, notably, that there exists a minimum threshold for their energy levels. Furthermore, I've established a direct relationship between this threshold and the moment of inertia in a specific type of system, composed of an elliptical body and a mass. I've also been able to establish, through a specific approximation, the necessary conditions under which this 'three plus three' state is the lowest-energy state in a specific framework, and through numerical analysis, I've determined the exact conditions under which it is present in a specific system, even when other effects are taken into consideration. This model has been successfully applied to a wide range of problems involving the motion of bodies in various types of systems, such as those involving a maximum of two rotors, or a single body with an attached mass, or those consisting of two masses connected in a specific way.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly altered compared to their bulk counterparts, a phenomenon attributed to interfacial effects, a uniquely two-dimensional characteristic. In this study, researchers explore how a monolayer intercalation of potassium affects the interfacial reaction between a 0.7-nanometer tungsten trioxide film and a graphene layer grown on top of it via chemical vapor deposition. Through local electrostatic doping, they map the interfacial reaction and discover that potassium removal triggers a metamorphosis from a Wagner diffusion-controlled process to a continuous growth mode, ultimately leading to a tungsten diooxide layer with a uniquely two-dimensional tungsten sub-lattice stripe phase rich in holes.

In many natural phenomena, the type of diffusion is not standard, often leading to abnormal diffusion patterns. Describing such patterns solely with the normal diffusion equation can yield inaccurate results, making the fractional diffusion equation a more reliable alternative. By applying the Laplace transform and inverse Laplace transform methods, we can derive the solutions to the time-fractional advection-diffusion equation. These solutions are expressed using the time-fractional diffusion Green's function. Furthermore, the application of the high-order product integration formula allows us to numerically solve the time-fractional advection-dusion equation. A specific example is provided to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. We also explore the long-term fractional diffusion patterns, examining their connection to the time-space fractional advection-diffusion equation.

This study investigates the effects of a major cryptocurrency market manipulation - the cryptocurrency stable coin arbitrage - utilizing blockchain technology and data from the Bitcoin and Ethereum networks. Analyzing over two million transactions over more than three years, we discovered that stable coins function as a pivotal class of cryptocurrency. They're created through complex, deceptive methods by criminals who also use private keys for illicit purposes including money laundering and financing. The arbitrage operation has primarily been carried out by a single group that heavily influences cryptocurrency prices and market stability in collaboration with major exchange insiders. This insider connection gives them exclusive access to and early information about new coins. Consequently, this has led to significant financial losses for retail investors, but substantial profits for the insider group.

The formation of clouds is initiated by droplets developing in connection to condensation nuclei when they reach a certain point in their development process. Through laboratory experiments and numerical simulations, researchers have studied how water develops on the surface of particles composed of various substances, such as seawater salts, organic compounds, and sulfur particles. To achieve this, they used special simulations that mimic the development of particles at extremely low temperatures typical of forming clouds. These experiments found that a vast number of substances develop into the forming particles when the environment's pressure increases, following the classic models used in the field of cloud formation. However, the findings also suggest that another type of particle known as ice nuclei may use different mechanisms for both ice and water development, which is important for understanding how ice forms first in particles at extremely low temperatures. Since cloud formation experiments can't test how changes in temperature affects the development of particles, more research at temperatures near room temperature has confirmed that the traditional models accurately predict how particles develop when the environment's pressure increases. As the particles develop, the position of the particles' surfaces shifts to match the growing particles, causing the environment's temperature near the surfaces to increase slightly as the model moves into the non-ice-related models. These changes in temperature and environment have implications for other components of cloud formation models, such as the development of particle-related water at low temperatures, the role of ice and water-related particles, and the effect of particle-related water on the development of new particles, which may influence how

We establish the definitions of a compact perception pair and a totally bounded measurement space to analyze sequences of functions from metric spaces to metric spaces that maintain uniform domain coverage and image metric consistency. Our findings demonstrate the equivalence of a map being a descending sequence to it being a limit sequence under specific conditions, and we provide a theory of convergence for maps under conditions where their images can be rescaled to converge in their original form. This and our previous work on ascending sequences to single maps complement each other and can be used to develop methods of reducing sequences of functions to singular objects, or 'shapes', representing sequences of perceptions or measurements. Our methods enable new, shape-theoretic converges for various objects like flexible measure spaces, free objects generated by maps from a set, and certain valuated metric spaces, and we provide a general valuated metric space theory of these converges. Our methods also have an application in interpreting infinite objects as completions of their finite parts in various contexts. Our theory of flexible measure spaces is revised and corrected, and our methods are applied in various new contexts to develop new shapes or valuated shapes for a variety of objects like flexible measure spaces and certain valuated metric spaces. Our methods are applicable in various new contexts and develop new shapes or valuated shapes for a variety of objects, including flexible measure spaces, free objects generated by maps from a set into a flexible measure space, and certain valuated metric spaces, and are applicable in various new contexts and develop new shapes or val

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space time. In this context, researchers have created theoretical models that integrate quantum mechanics and relativistic principles to study how different types of matter, such as non-relativistic fermions and Dirac fermions, move when influenced by gravity. In these systems, the flow of energy across surfaces at different elevations is significantly affected by the variation in gravitational potential. As a result, the energy flow appears to move towards the area with the higher gravitational potential, giving the impression of a downward flow of heat. Notably, this phenomenon can lead to observable effects when considering the flow of spin and charge in materials like mercury and graphite.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been quite limited, and we propose using manifold theory to define a model's complexity, drawing connections between complexity and the subspace in which data is collected and the curved manifold representing the data's distribution. For neural network training, we establish a method to achieve any desired manifold shape, and through analysis, discover that training involves alternating between moving within the subspace (simplest case) or adjusting the manifold shape (general case), and that sufficient complexity is always allocated to represent the subspace or the adjusted manifold, respectively. For specific types of complexity, such as that required for solution accuracy, we provide a general method, and for regularization-driven complexity, such as from L2 or dropout, we express complexity as a product of original complexity and an exponential function, dependent on the amount of regularization used.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and LHCb's upcoming Run 2 dataset.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing. Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable difficulties such as the need to evaluate samples of a relatively small size and the lack of a consistent standard to measure accuracy. In this study, we focus on employing pre-trained transformer models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, in order to boost the accuracy of essay grading. Specifically, we investigate using these models in combination with traditional LSTMs and attention mechanisms, as well as using them independently to make predictions. Our results indicate that leveraging pre-trained models can substantially boost the accuracy of essay grading, with pre-LSTMs providing only an auxiliary function and pre-trained models acting more effectively on their own. Our code and data are available on GitHub at the link in the reference section.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginal independence model, we explore specific conditions under which the model can be simplified into a toric model using a linear transformation, similar to the approach taken in earlier research on Baumgartner et al's and Sato et al's theorem. This text presents a new, direct method for achieving this simplification through coordinate transformations.

A higher education system plays a crucial role in promoting social mobility across different generations.  To analyze this, we develop a model that incorporates two mechanisms: (i) mobility through inheritance of talents and (ii) mobility through the distribution of human-capital producing inputs.  Our model suggests that policies aiming to enhance mobility must not only consider measures that affect the flow of talent between generations but also the flow of educational resources.  To achieve this, such policies may need to counteract a tendency towards the equalization of educational resources between generations, even in the presence of existing inequality.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

Our ring signature-based Delegated RingCT allows multiple parties to collaborate on securing a decentralized cryptocurrency by combining key materials to form group keys, which can be used to sign transactions.  The DEDEE Delegated Ethereum Explorer is a full de-centralized web application, using React for the UI framework and IPFS for content storage, that serves as both a demonstration tool and educational platform for Delegated RingCT implementations.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set, containing 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information at 13 TeV.  Five distinct end states were studied to look for this rare occurrence.  When analyzing all data, the probability of this discovery being due to random fluctuations is calculated at 5.2 standard deviations.  After careful examination, the data align with theoretical predictions to a degree, showing only a minor discrepancy.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This old corpus is insufficient for developing robust NLP models capable of handling contemporary Hebrew. To address this issue, our study combines, cleans, and expands the corpus, simpling the grammar to create T Hebrew, a new parsed treebank comprising straightforward sentences drawn from TurT. Additionally, we integrated T Hebrew, into HeTReB, a comprehensive Hebrew NLP benchmark corpus.

We maintain in L_p its natural norm, considering the space L_p as consisting of functions defined on a certain set with values realizable as functions from a limited set of m elements in L_2. Our research demonstrates that for any function within L_p defined by the maximum of the functions from L_2, there exists an isometric reduction of its dimension to m, which we also show can be achieved for functions defined by their epsilon approximation as well as for functions defined by their epsilon lower bound, which we also extend to be applicable in L_1 and for functions defined by the sum as well as to Lipschitz functions defined on a limited set of m elements in L_2, which we demonstrate can be reduced isometrically to an epsilon level with a dimension that exceeds m only by a factor that increases logarithmically. This reduction is also shown to be optimal for the sum, which we also show can be compressed in a space that exceeds m only by a factor that increases logarithmically, which we also show can be compressed for Lipschitz functions in a space that exceeds m only by a factor that increases polynomially, which we also show can be compressed for any function within L_2, for which there exists an isometric reduction of its dimension to m only in a way that exceeds m by a factor that increases polynomially, which we also show can be compressed for any function within L_p defined by the sum as well as to any Lipschitz function

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have fueled their widespread adoption in applications like computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, and decision-making systems. As their complexity grows through the addition of new data, a problem arises where previous information is overlooked, leading to a decline in performance on prior tasks. This phenomenon, known as catastrophic forgetting, poses a significant obstacle. In response, researchers are actively developing various continual learning strategies. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of several popular approaches in this field, offering a comprehensive review and comparing their effectiveness. As a result, it serves as a valuable reference for future research and development in this burgeoning area of study.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually employ statistical ensemble theory to evaluate their threshold transmission rates over binary erasure channels. This research develops a more advanced method for predicting the conditional typical hargreaves rate of binary erasure channels, taking into account the correlations between link transmissions. Using this new approach, we derive the typical transmission rate for LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. Our findings show that the optimal transmission rate can be achieved by combining specific statistical models involving correlations between link transmissions. Further investigation into the optimal performance of correlated LDPC ensembles reveals that the optimal transmission rate can be achieved by combining specific statistical models involving correlations between link transmissions. Simulations also confirm that the optimal transmission rate can be significantly surpassed by incorporating correlations between link transmissions. This new approach may have practical applications in improving data transmission using LDPC codes.

An advanced modular system, which can prevent collisions in unpredictable environments, utilizes data from complex interactions between objects. This modular safety filter system, which is built on predictive control, is enhanced by incorporating an optimized control strategy that covers all possible controls. Current methods use approximate techniques based on the L1-norm, which lack precision. In response, a new method is proposed that provides more accurate results, which, in addition, requires less computational resources. Simulations using car following scenarios have shown the new method, which, compared to traditional L1-norm approaches, offers better safety, precision, and computational efficiency.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) due to its vulnerability to attacks exploiting device defects and implementation errors. Researchers have devised the concept of coherent detection QKD to enhance device efficiency and mitigate the impact of vulnerabilities. Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether this approach can entirely resolve the problem until a complete and experimentally validated model of the quantum channel has been established. In this study, we propose a novel method to accurately estimate the average quantum state vector $\vert \psi_{A\rightarrow B}\rangle_{av}$ of the recipient's quantum channel by analyzing coherent pulses without detecting individual photons. By combining this model with tomographic techniques, we can determine the average quantum state vector $\vert \psi_{A\rightarrow B}\rangle_{av}$ with high precision. Employing our developed models, we successfully simulated the full QKD process using the BB84 protocol by constructing realistic channels without individual photons. Furthermore, our modeling approach yielded secure keys using realistic detection noise parameters, validating the effectiveness of our decision model even under challenging conditions.

Recent studies on large language models have highlighted in-context learning (ICL), a short-term adaptive mechanism that allows models to quickly adjust to various down-stream tasks.  The potential of ICL, such as its ability to tackle previously unseen tasks with strong generalization and model choice flexibility, has attracted significant interest.  The goal of this study is to investigate the factors that influence the performance of ICL, with a focus on the effects of pretraining corpus on model learning and adaptation.  The study examines the relationship between pretraining data, model representation, and the internal mechanisms of ICL, using diverse evaluation metrics and analytical approaches.  The findings suggest that certain features of the pretraining corpus, including its source, content balance, and data distribution, significantly impact the model's learning and generalization abilities.  Specifically, it is observed that: (i) synthetic data enhances model learning; (ii) certain pretraining corpora contain more beneficial information for ICL; (iii) improving content balance in pretraining data leads to better generalization; and (iv) different pretraining data sources result in varying activation patterns and internal mechanisms for ICL.  Overall, the study sheds light on the critical role of pretraining data in shaping the model's short-term learning abilities.

Galaxy cluster observations have revealed evidence of massive cold clouds within their intergalactic space, yet the mechanisms behind their formation, development, composition, and final destruction remain unclear. We conducted a comprehensive simulation, using high-resolution data to analyze the behavior of these giant intergalactic clouds within a galaxy cluster's hot environment, focusing on cooling processes. Our model tracked the temporal and spatial evolution of cold clouds, confirming that metal-poor clouds form quickly, last longer, and maintain lower temperatures, making them detectable with current instruments. Conversely, clouds forming primarily through cooling are short-lived, as heat is efficiently re-emitted, rendering them difficult to detect. We also discovered the influence of local gravity on cold clouds, which causes them to collapse and move towards the cluster's center of gravity, resulting in the absorption of hot intergalactic gas and subsequent heating or fragmentation. Ultimately, hot upflows or mergers destroy or disperse these cold clouds, making understanding of hot gas dynamics crucial for predicting cloud behavior. We deemed self-shielding a minor factor, as it has little impact on cold clouds' development when formulating guidelines for interpreting future intergalactic cloud observations.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty hadron decays serves as a crucial test for the expected behavior of the Standard Model. This examination also serves as a sensitive indicator for potential anomalies that could be attributed to new physical phenomena occurring at high energy scales. The precision with which this examination can be conducted within reach at hadron collars has now attained a level that makes future discoveries more certain. This text serves as a summary of the current status of $C\!P$ violation examinations in beauty hadron decays achieved by the LHCb collaboration, supplemented by other collaborations.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory using exceptional properties of the long-range symmetry $psl(2|1)^\infty$. To establish $psl(2|1)^\infty$ as a fundamental aspect of superstrings, its low-energy relevance in the long strings regime has also been investigated. A closed-form expression for low-energy four-point on-shell generators of $psl(2|1)^\infty$ in the lightcone gauge was successfully derived, utilizing the known supertransformations as a starting point. Interestingly, this expression diverges in four-point process due to an anomaly in the commutator with the supertranslation generator within the $psl(2|1)^\infty$ algebra, echoing similar behavior in its bosonic counterpart observed at low energies.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data and resources in upcoming mobile networks, advanced analytical techniques like forecasting and optimization are crucial. By incorporating machine learning into resource allocation, these techniques can optimize resource usage while adapting to specific constraints. Deep reinforcement learning, a sophisticated form of learning, stands out as a leading approach for resource allocation in complex networks. Though reinforcement learning has been used in resource allocation for some time, the novel integration of quantum computing is only beginning to be explored in this area. Due to its rapid computational speed, quantum computing is well-suited for handling the complexity of massive networks. However, the fully quantum approach is limited by hardware constraints, which has led to the development of hybrid quantum-classical methods. Hybrid quantum-classical variational approaches are being tested for their potential in simple communication problems, but a comprehensive evaluation of their application to future network resources is needed. Therefore, this work introduces an innovative hybrid quantum-classical model for resource allocation in advanced mobile networks, utilizing a hybrid graph neural network variant and a quantum variational circuit optimizer to efficiently manage the complexity of these networks.

Our zero-speech speech synthesis system operates without audio training data, by drawing on the acoustic features of pre-trained speech models to create "phonemes," "diphonemes," and other fundamental units. These are then combined with learned transformations to generate more complex structures like "phoneme sequences" and "audio sequences." This strategy enables us to substantially enhance the quality of speech synthesis, by substantially improving the likelihood of pho

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested in various 3-DOF robot configurations, demonstrating consistent results compared to industry-standard nonlinear solvers with a statistical analysis confirming its superiority.

We have developed two transformation methods, both deterministic and probabilistic, 
for quantum states using quantum operations in certain resource theories. 
To determine the necessary conditions for these transformations, 
which are not always sufficient, 
our approach employs a geometric interpretation within the framework of the underlying quantum theory. 
Furthermore, 
by introducing a stronger form of physical transformation, 
which retains the relevant quantum correlations in a subset of the system, 
we have established a sufficient condition for achieving probabilistic transformation of quantum states. 
The application of our derived criteria is demonstrated in specific instances within known quantum theories.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The results showed that a single form of excitation can induce instability in the pendulum's steady state, while combined exposure leads to the induction of horizontal and period-doubling bifurcations.

In our research paper, we introduce a new communication-efficient technique called Dr-Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) for handling the distributed optimization of problems with uncertain constraints. By incorporating the concept of distributionally robust convex optimization with uncertain constraints, our approach optimizes a problem under a broad range of probability distributions over the noise affecting decentralized optimization. Dr-DSGD achieves better empirical performance and a guaranteed tolerance to noise in communication compared to a basic DSGD method. To expedite convergence, our proposal utilizes the Duality Gap Minimization (DGM) technique, which has a proven linear convergence rate in certain cases, and adapts it to address uncertainty in problems with uncertain constraints via the Lagrangian function and its dual constraints.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the typical delay in reaching thermal equilibrium and how it affects the properties of particles formed.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, we study how strong magnetic fields interact with star-forming regions and their jets. To achieve this, we ran a series of simulations with varying levels of magnetic field strength, specifically 0, 0.05, 0.1, and 0.2 times the mass magnetic field ratio, differing from previous studies that often used lower levels.

Our findings show that without a magnetic field, a star-forming cloud forms multiple stars, with material ejected in unorganized outflows.

The introduction of a magnetic field alters this behavior, causing star-forming clouds to become aligned with magnetic field lines, delaying star formation by causing protostellar jets to become collated only during the main phase of star formation.

Our research indicates that the formation of flat structures, often seen in star-forming regions, is primarily driven by gravitational instability, rather than magnetic fields, and our analysis confirms that this alignment can occur under various magnetic conditions.

We found that the magnetic field strength significantly impacts the behavior of protostellar jets, with strongly magnetized clouds producing jets that align with magnetic field lines, pass through the forming star, and emerge from the surrounding cloud, causing their surfaces to appear bright due to the emission of gas, and causing their widths to be narrower than those of non-magnetized jets, than those of non-magnetized jets.

Our analysis suggests that protostellar jets can be a result of both magnetic fields and

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations in complex nonlinear systems governed by convex constraints. A novel approach, inspired by value management principles, is introduced to inform decision-making processes. To address these decisions, a specialized value function is developed, which is equivalent to an integrated performance assessment and safety evaluation framework. The performance evaluation component aggregates multiple output signals through a multi-attributive utility function, whereas the safety assessment component aggregates various safety constraints using a multi-attributive safety function. Decision making is facilitated by optimizing a combined value function that incorporates both components. To account for system nonlinearities and uncertain dynamics, a generalized uncertainty description is used. Moreover, specific properties of the safety function are defined to ensure that safety constraints can be managed efficiently across a wide range of system behaviors. It is demonstrated, under specific conditions, that the proposed approach allows the safe operating range to be linearly partitioned into discrete intervals. As system trajectories shift due to control adjustments, real-time scaling of the allowed performance level can be achieved by referencing these predefined safety ranges. The described framework is demonstrated through its application to a flight control system.

This research explores the equilibrium points of objects experiencing a significant gravitational pull from the Earth, taking into consideration the impact of solar radiation and varying rates of expansion. For objects with a high area-to-mass ratio, the Earth's non-uniform gravitational field significantly influences their behavior, unlike previous models that neglected the effect of their expansion rate. A mathematical model is developed to describe the motion of these objects, known as the Lagrangian equations of the Hill-Rectified Quadrupole System, in an inertial frame of reference. By expanding the model into two distinct components, its dynamics can be analyzed more effectively through averaging techniques, ultimately simplifying the model into the restricted three-body problem format. This study identifies conditions under which stable points exist in the system and identifies the emergence of unique periodic orbits in the process. Additionally, the research identifies the existence of at least seven equilibrium points in the simplified model and identifies the locations of their stable points, which change significantly based on the area-to-mass ratio of the object. Furthermore, the investigation into the stability of these equilibrium points reveals areas of uncertainty concerning their behavior, which cannot be determined through conventional methods, including the presence of both stable and unstable equilibrium points, which may interchange characteristics under certain conditions, including the loss or gain of point stability.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principles principles. The conventional method of representing the vector potential in such models, often adopted from electronic structure theory, turns out to be incompatible with the tight-binding framework itself. Building upon earlier findings, we introduce a modified approach for describing the interaction between light and matter in tight-binding models, grounded in the principles of the dipole gauge rather than the velocity gauge, which yields more accurate and physically consistent results. We evaluate the performance of this new "dipole gauge tight-binding" approach against the more traditional "velocity gauge tight-binding" method in various scenarios, including electron emission, localized excitations, and collective responses, and demonstrate that it delivers better outcomes. Furthermore, we develop and apply a method for efficiently computing two-photon absorption spectra using the newly proposed approach, achieving results in good agreement with exact solutions while being computationally more feasible.

In this research, our objective is to provide a precise 3D pose and shape assessment of point clouds in the presence of substantial intra-class variations. To accomplish this, our proposed framework employs a combination of point correspondence and optimal transport theory to derive shape-based depth maps from 2D images. By utilizing these depth maps as reference templates, our method effectively reduces variability and facilitates accurate pose and shape estimation through alignment procedures. Furthermore, our framework utilizes a multi-scale strategy that enables it to accommodate various object scales and serves as a versatile shape-based registration approach that can be applied to general 3D point cloud registration tasks. Extensive evaluations of general and category-level pose and shape recovery demonstrate the exceptional efficacy of our proposed framework.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as pairs of real numbers $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ representing intervals for both parameters.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under the assumption that they share the same treatment response mechanism. This approach tracks the treatment response in each arm over time and uses this information to make more accurate comparisons, providing better reliability as more data are collected. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method is comparable to traditional approaches, but exhibits superior performance in specific scenarios, such as when response rates are high or when there is little difference between control and treatment options. This method will be implemented in an ongoing two-stage trial comparing the immunotherapy agent LS-0 in various tumor types to determine its potential as a standalone treatment or in combination with chemotherapy.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed to an extremely high standard of accuracy and speed efficiency in real-time, particularly in situations influenced by external disturbances and variable operating conditions. However, the current control design strategies often prioritize performance in the frequency domain, neglecting complex multi-peaks resonance characteristics and variable operating points, leading to a trade-off between accuracy and dynamic performance. This study introduces a novel time-based feedback control method, utilizing iterative learning to compensate for system dynamics and improve overall performance, particularly in high-precision motion systems.

We introduce a universal, keypoint-based approach for aligning partial keypoint sets within point cloud spaces. Our novel learning framework simultaneously detects keypoints and their corresponding orientations, and we employ alignment loss to improve orientation consistency. To speed up processing, a detector is utilized to locate keypoints on input meshes, and these are then utilized in orientation estimation. Our approach is characterized by outstanding accuracy and a rapid processing speed, achieved through efficient network architecture and detection mechanism.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if every twist $\alpha$ of G produces an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. The number of such classes is denoted as $R_\infty(\alpha)$. The count is referred to as the $R_\infty$-invariant. The current study examines the structure of $R_\infty$-invariants across various group types. For instance, if G has a subgroup N that is finitely generated and torsion-free, then the total count of twist classes within the quotient group G/N is no greater than the sum of those in N and G/GN$. Additionally, when a short exact sequence 1 -> N -> G -> Q -> 1 is given where Q is finitely generated, our findings provide a precise lower limit for the total count of twist classes in G, which is determined by the interaction between Q's automorphisms and N's outer auto-transformations. This is supported by a more comprehensive theorem that applies to a wider variety of exact sequences. The results are particularly useful in calculating the $R_\infty$-invariant for a large assortment of group examples. This review provides an overview of how precise measurements can offer insight into various theoretical problems through their influence on the Standard Model, particularly within the context of effective field theories. The paper focuses on three critical areas where the mass of the top quark, the dimensions of boson self-couplings, and the dimensions of Higgs-boson coupling to other particles play a pivotal role. We will examine the potential solutions to these issues via the mechanisms of technical naturalness and accidental naturalness.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, and $K^*$, as well as the distribution transverse polarizations, for the $D$ and $K$ mesons. Furthermore, we explain the concept of light-front distribution amplitudes for vector mesons in both longitudinal and transverse states, and present the explicit expressions for calculating the T-odd distribution functions $H_d$ and $W_\perp$ for the vector mesons. Notably, our findings reveal a significant variation in the T-odd distribution functions for the $K^+$ and $D^+$ mesons, which could have a significant impact on the calculation of the electric dipole angle in the $K^+$ $\to$ $\pi^+$ decay and possibly even be tested experimentally.

This article provides further investigation into the properties of bounded subspaces associated with the tempered modulation and Fourier transform, specifically examining their restrictions to certain sets and the resulting spaces' nontriviality under specific conditions.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address specific, established modalities, ignoring diverse medical images or requiring a substantial number of labeled instances for adaptation. This paper presents a novel approach to instance segmentation of previously encountered images modalities by leveraging knowledge from related images, even with very limited annotations. The method utilizes known unlabeled instances to inform the segmentation of instance features in a new, partially annotated image modality through example-based learning. The experimental results obtained on synthetic data demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to fully supervised segmentation, even with as few as five annotated training samples.

Our proposed algorithm leverages the power of deep learning to implement a sophisticated action recognition system without the need for a fully trained classifier. It uses a small, hand-crafted recurrent neural network to predict future video features, which are then used to identify the most likely action and simulate the backtracking process to optimize classification. This novel approach uses the RNN to learn the dynamics of video data, which we demonstrate to be a useful tool for action classification in our implementation. Additionally, we've designed our network architecture to be action-specific and used feature vectors that are easily accessible, which results in significant space and time savings for breaking the existing state-of-the-art performance on standard action recognition benchmarks at just one frame or up to one second later.

High-energy flares emitted by small stars pose a significant challenge to the habitability of exoplanets, potentially interfering with detecting biosignatures. Despite this, little is known about the characteristics of white-light flares during the early stages of planetary system development. This study presents the detection of a white-light flare from K2-3, a known exoplanet host star, observed using the Transiting Planet Survey Satellite. By analyzing these flares in conjunction with other tools like TESS and KOI, it was possible to determine their power and frequency distribution, which can help inform our understanding of the conditions affecting planetary systems during their early stages.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. Our analysis shows that the obstruction to this deformation lies within the cohomology group $H^1_{\mu}{\check{C}}$ of the bundle ${\check{C}}$, which represents the spinor bundle associated with the nearly G2-structure on a seven-dimensional manifold $M$. The cohomology $H^1_{\mu}{\check{C}}$ is not typically relevant as it is usually equal to zero; this implies that the underlyign cohomology group $H^1_M{\mathcal Hs}(E)$, representing the obstruction to the deformation of an G2-instanton on a G2-manifold $M$, is the relevant obstruction in most cases. We also prove that locally commutative families of G2-instantons exist.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models are commonly used in classification and detection tasks involving 3D data, but they struggle with high-dimensional transformation tasks. We introduce a series of common 3D transformations as a benchmark and evaluate the current state-of-the-art models as a baseline. From this assessment, we discover that existing models cannot handle these challenges, leading us to propose a simple yet effective approach, incorporating U-Net with random rotation augmentation, 3D volume-based input, and unique optimization methods, to improve their performance. Our strategy consistently outperforms other methods in both the NuScenes and Oxford-ROBOTH datasets in both classification and detection applications. To further boost accuracy, we introduce three additional techniques: KNN-based evaluation, the use of high-frequency features for U-Unit design, and the implementation of the multi-scale, multi-order, and random-patch training strategy for 3D rotation transformation.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar networks with multiple radars accessing the same area simultaneously. Since radar signals are deterministic, we utilize clear channel assessment (CCA) in our Coordinated Time Division Multiple Access (Co-TDMA) scheme to enhance its efficiency. To resolve contentions, we implement a neighbor discovery and identification process to obtain the necessary information for the CCA. The CCA in our Co-TDMA scheme involves scanning 360 degrees by measuring phase distance with neighboring radars in a sector by sector manner. We develop a novel Co-TDMA protocol and conduct extensive simulations based on FMCW settings to evaluate its contention resolution capabilities. The outcomes demonstrate that our Co-TDMA protocol can successfully identify the location of contenting radars and avoid package interference by adjusting transmission timing, while ensuring optimal utilization of time slots. Additionally, we outline a method to mitigate potential errors in the estimated radar locations to maintain transmission synchronization.

Our investigation explores the theoretical and experimental possibilities for observing entropy ordering in a joint measurement of photons, a phenomenon that may arise from their interaction with a special kind of "entangled photon transistor." The resulting correlations of these photons, known as the second-order correlation function, were investigated experimentally using a entangled pair of photons and a quantum dot as an optical amplifier. The outcomes of these experiments are consistent with an analogy between these photons and quantum mechanics particles, which could open up new avenues for exploring quantum phenomena and developing new applications of entangled photons.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre99 satisfies the axioms outlined in AGZ21 and AGZ22 and an additional T-weight assumption.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate temporal event and knowledge graph rules. This study explores
the application of this problem in event and time-series analysis by formulating
it as completing a temporal knowledge graph of events by predicting missing event
times. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative method called
TeKGC, an autonomous and multi-stage approach that decomposes the issue into
two subproblems: event alignment and link prediction. To solve the first subproblem,
TeKGC employs a hierarchical model that distinguishes between events that are
significant and those that are not. For the second subproblem, TeKGC utilises a
time-aware model to take into account the event alignment status and any time-related
patterns within the temporal knowledge graph. For evaluation, we conducted
experiments on two real-world datasets and the results show that TeKGC outperforms
several existing baseline completion methods in terms of both event alignment
accuracy and link prediction precision.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, derived from a semi-analytical analytical model, is used to examine the significance of ground sound under certain assumptions. An analytical approach allows for the calculation of the impact source's radiated sound and the source on the ground via a double dipole representation. By applying the same parameters as a previous study, the relationship between the radiated sound and the source's perceived sound is analyzed using two perceived frequency criteria. It is found that ground sound is more perceptible at low frequencies, though its contribution may not be as substantial as that of the air radiated sound. Additionally, the semi-analytical model reveals that, in many scenarios, ground sound is heavily affected by vertical impact directions and is significantly attenuated due to the presence of an image source. These findings help to identify the limitations ground sound recognition on rigid bodies may have, informing the development of future models and the understanding of potential errors in predicted values.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality involves all-versus-nothing (AVN) proofs, which unequivocally reveal the limitations of local hidden variable theories. Notably, such proofs can be categorised into two types: Type A, showcasing the inevitability of Bell nonlocality from a global perspective, and Type B, illustrating its inevitability when examining subsets of parties. Previous research has exclusively concentrated on perfect correlations enabling Type A and Type B all-versus-nothing proofs. However, this study introduces novel concepts, i.e., imperfect-type all-versus-nothing proofs, accounting for the impact of imperfect correlations on Bell nonlocality demonstrations. Two distinct approaches to creating such proofs are proposed: Type A all-versus-nothing proofs involving one measurement configuration and Type B all-versus-nothing proofs involving multiple measurements. Moreover, quantitative standards for the strength of these proofs relative to proof depth are introduced. Our investigation delves into the depth of Bell nonlocality demonstrations across various scenarios, including multipartite Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, genuine multipartite nonlocality in specific scenarios, and real-world experiments. Moreover, we present a method for quantifying the strength of Bell nonlocality in terms of proof depth.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by itinerancy dynamics. Current understanding in condensed matter physics mainly stems from experimental studies, whereas theoretical insights are often based on models assuming exact solvability. However, one crucial class of exactly solvable models with high relevance to experimental results has yet to be comprehensively described theoretically - the multiband dimer model, which accurately describes various phenomena in different physical settings. This work introduces a general framework for multiband dimer models and identifies conditions under which they remain exactly solvable through gauge-invariant conditions. Notably, this framework reveals that while two-level multiband dimer models are always exactly solvable, higher-level models may not be. In cases where higher-level models are exactly solvable, theoretical tools have been developed to investigate ground state properties, higher temperatures, and dynamic behavior, with examples provided using two-level and three-level multiband dimer models.

Using first-principles calculations, I discover a potential hydrogen boride monolayer superconductor with the 3×3×1 rhombic prism lattice, exhibiting considerable in-plane thermal stability and stability against crystal distortion. Hydrogen atoms in this structure act as electron donors, transferring charge to the boron sublattice and enabling the boron d$x^2$-$y^2$ and $dZ^2$ orbitals to contribute to hydrogen boride monolayer superconductivity. Hydrogen boride monolayer exhibits superior electron-phonon coupling and stronger superconducting properties compared to h-BN and hydrided graphene. Additionally, it has the advantage of being experimentally feasible to create through hydrogen monolayer epitaxial deposition on hexagonal boron nitride.

Research on the division of sets into portions continues to gain importance, particularly in areas exploring the splitting of these divisions into two parts where the characteristics of each segment can be measured. The research focuses on a specific classification scheme that involves splitting the division of a set into n parts into two segments, each containing n elements, and it uses the lexicographical comparison to establish an order, ultimately leading to the development of a distinct classification that is used to establish the total number of possible divisions into these segments for a set consisting of n labeled elements.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of randomness in a broad setting of changes over time, covering cases like transitions between states and patterns forming in materials. To do this, we've created a measure of "hardness" for these transitions, which helps us understand how complex the system's behavior is. Using this measurement, can make or break a certain type of randomness, causing it to behave differently. It turns out that in many systems with this measurement, there's a limited set of equilibrium points, and the change between these points is as complicated as the surface of the numbers themselves. Additionally, this measurement provides a significant distinction between the behavior of the surface and other, softer forms of randomness.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system must swiftly take over control from a failing primary system without compromising overall safety. Implementing fail-operational redundancy demands comprehensive testing and validation of E/E systems. To validate these systems, dynamic and functional tests are used to trigger failing components, but a critical gap exists in methods for validating the backup switch itself. To fill this void, a novel approach is introduced that leverages non-invasive injection of a random data pattern into the communication network, forcing the target component to fail and testing the backup switch and backup component's responses. The introduced method is then used to evaluate a drive-by-wire system, successfully implementing a speed control failure and triggering the backup component to restore the controlled speed. To drive the target component into failure, a safety management function is used to oversee and ensure safe operation throughout the process.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by employing a time-series clustering algorithm that utilizes the Cross-Correlation Mutual Information (CCMI) metric as a proxy time-series feature and applies the K-means-means-shift (K-means-ms) measure to improve the clustering of small sample sizes. The proposed method Cross-Correlation Mutual Information K-means-means-shift (CCMI-K-means-ms) demonstrates enhanced clustering results compared to existing alternatives such as Cross-Entropy based K-means and PCA based Cross-Entropy K-means, particularly for identifying relevant lags in dynamic systems and clustering time-series data sets. The comparison with state-of-the-art techniques like CCMI-PSC-ENKMEANS and CAMeS also reveals the proposed method's capacity to produce superior result and run-time efficiency. The successful application of the proposed method on synthetic and real-world data sets further validates its suitability for identifying correlated variables and dynamic clustering of time-series data.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describing its mathematical processes.  Many scholars have evaluated the merits of geometric versus algebraic representations; a key argument being that foundations should not rely on a particular domain's specific terms.  However, this review argues that scholarly evaluation of the algebraic route is insufficient, particularly concerning modern interpretations that prioritize geometric understandings.  Instead, it highlights an overlooked set of algebraic tools - polynomial approximation - which this article seeks to re-examine within the context of Leibnizian calculus.  By delving into recent scholarship on the subject, this review sheds light on contemporary interpretations of polynomial approximation, particularly its reliance on the B\"uchner principle, while also addressing concerns regarding its universal applicability.

Using the Euclid HI intensity mapping multi-dimensional power spectrum analysis that combines machine learning techniques with a Bayesian framework to simultaneously estimate non-linear bias coefficients and cosmological parameters from simulated data with realistic noise levels.
